Before connecting a new generation unit to an electrical network, an operator needs to know how currents will redistribute and whether any line will overload. Testing every proposed connection on the real network is impractical and could cause the failure we want to avoid. The proposed network has not yet produced measurements, and measurements from the existing network may leave some currents unobserved. Prediction therefore requires reusable component laws and an estimate of the hidden state. Likewise, a model trained on one four-legged robot typically mispredicts another with different mass, leg lengths and motors, so each new robot needs fresh data and retraining.

We introduce C-PHAST, a compositional port-Hamiltonian world model for predicting the physical consequences of proposed configurations. Extending our single-system model PHAST, it learns how each component type stores and dissipates energy, connects components through power-preserving ports, and estimates unobserved states from measurement histories. Given proposed wiring and initial states for added components, it predicts the resulting dynamics without retraining. Connections can also create behavior no component shows alone. For known linear systems, we show when one component's damping drains energy from another and when an existing sensor can better estimate a hidden state elsewhere. We also derive error margins under which predictions certify which of two proposed configurations scores better.

In simulated DC microgrids, given the same data and starting states as prior compositional port-Hamiltonian neural networks, C-PHAST predicts unseen five-unit networks with over 40-fold lower voltage error, in a comparison of complete training procedures that differ in model family, initialization, objective and integrator. From noisy voltage histories, it reduces hidden-current error by 67.6% relative to CT-SUBNET, a black-box state-space model. In simulated zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer, a leg model learned only on ANYmal-D is reused unchanged on Unitree Go2 and never told how Go2 differs; a short history of Go2 joint positions sets only its starting state, and its error grows 1.6-fold, against 21-fold for a recurrent network that fits ANYmal-D better. Four-joint arm models also transfer zero-shot to two to eight joints. On real Spot-with-arm logs, a predictor built on its physical readouts retrospectively estimates joint work and battery draw (Pearson r >= 0.94). Each capability is tested separately; ranking configurations with learned laws from partial measurements remains open. Learning laws for components, not whole systems, is a step toward world models that predict a configuration before it is built.
